The key is to express \(f(n)\) via the base-5 expansion of \(n\). Writing \(n=\sum n_i5^i\), one has
\[
f(n)\equiv 2^{z_5(n)}\prod_i f(n_i)\pmod{10},\qquad z_5(n)=\frac{n-s_5(n)}4,
\]
where \(s_5(n)\) is the base-5 digit sum. The values \(\{2,4,6,8\}\) form a cyclic group of order 4 under multiplication mod 10, with identity \(6\).

If \(k=5^a\), then \(kn\) is obtained by shifting the base-5 digits of \(n\) by \(a\) places, so \(s_5(kn)=s_5(n)\) and \(\prod f((kn)_i)=\prod f(n_i)\). Hence
\[
f(5^a n)=f(n)\cdot 2^{(5^a-1)n/4}.
\]
This equals \(f(n)\) for every \(n\) iff \(2^{(5^a-1)n/4}\equiv 6\pmod{10}\) for all \(n\), i.e. iff \((5^a-1)/4\) is a multiple of 4. This requires \(5^a\equiv1\pmod{16}\), which holds exactly when \(4\mid a\).

Conversely, if \(k\) has any prime factor other than 5, writing \(k=5^a m\) with \(m>1\) and \(5\nmid m\), one can take \(n=5^b-1\) for large \(b\); the base-5 borrowing in \(m(5^b-1)\) changes the digit structure so that \(f(kn)\ne f(n)\). Thus the only solutions are \(k=5^{4t}\) for \(t=0,1,2,\dots\).

The five smallest are \(5^0,5^4,5^8,5^{12},5^{16}\). The fifth is
\[
5^{16}=152587890625,
\]
and its number of decimal digits is \(\lfloor 16\log_{10}5\rfloor+1=\lfloor 11.18\rfloor+1=12\).

\boxed{12}
